thread.title: How tax and accounting changes obscured a strong quarter for earnings - MarketWatch

author: Ciara Linnane ,     Tomi Kilgore ,   and   Francine McKenna
title: How tax and accounting changes obscured a strong quarter for earnings - MarketWatch
text:
The earnings season that’s now drawing to a close has been a bit of a blur.
The tax bill signed into law in December introduced a new layer of confusion to the usual muddle of GAAP and non-GAAP numbers, or those prepared under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles and those that adjust for one-time items.
Almost every company included in their fourth-quarter earnings reports disclosures of the noncash charges or gains they will book as they are forced to recalculate the value of tax assets or tax liabilities based on the lowering of the corporate tax rate to 21% from 35%.
But the law also imposes a transitional tax of 15.5% on reinvested earnings held as liquid assets overseas, and an 8% tax on reinvested earnings held as illiquid assets overseas. That tax will be a cash charge starting in 2018, although it can be paid in installments over the next eight years.
The Securities and Exchange Commission offered guidance on how companies should explain the impact of the tax bill on their 2017 earnings, directing them to report changes based on a “reasonable estimate” that can be adjusted later, as MarketWatch has reported.
‘In the past few years, aggressive non-GAAP adjustments were criticized more than once for masking significant expenses. Yet, in this case, companies almost have to exclude the one-time tax reform impact from the non-GAAP EPS data during earnings calls to give investors a more accurate picture of company’s earnings.’ Audit Analytics But companies took very different approaches to their disclosures, making it tricky for investors to figure out whether results had met, missed or beaten analysts’ estimates.
“In the past few years, aggressive non-GAAP adjustments were criticized more than once for masking significant expenses,” Audit Analytics wrote in a report. “Yet, in this case, companies almost have to exclude the one-time tax reform impact from the non-GAAP EPS data during earnings calls to give investors a more accurate picture of company’s earnings.”
See: Tax bill lowered corporate tax rate, so why are some companies announcing charges?
Related: New tax law spells big changes for companies’ approach to executive compensation
Audit Analytics analyzed regulatory filings for about 440 of the S&P 500 and found that four-fifths had adjusted their GAAP per-share earnings for the impact of the tax bill. Of those, 72% presented the adjusted number as a separate line item, while the remaining 28% combined it with other tax-related items, creating confusion for investors trying to compare the number to a prior period’s figure.
Time Warner Inc. TWX, -0.34% , for example, reported adjusted EPS of $2.66 versus $1.25 for the year-earlier period and way above the $1.44 consensus. But the number included a tax benefit of $1.06, without which the adjusted number would be a more comparable $1.60. (The company did not provide that adjustment in its release.)
Meanwhile, a FactSet analysis of earnings reports for the 30 components of the Dow Jones Industrial Average revealed the wide gap (no pun intended) between the GAAP earnings, GAAP earnings excluding tax charges or gains, and non-GAAP earnings excluding tax charges or benefits.
Twenty-eight Dow components disclosed charges or benefits, with only two — Apple Inc. AAPL, +0.87% and Nike Inc. NKE, +1.21% — failing to provide any number relating to the tax-code changes in their releases, according to FactSet senior earnings analyst John Butter.
FactSet gathered the GAAP EPS numbers, weighted them by shares outstanding, and then aggregated the share-weighted earnings number to arrive at a total GAAP earnings number of $42.2 billion for the Dow. It then calculated a GAAP EPS number that excluded the tax charge or gain to arrive at a new GAAP number of about $75.6 billion.
FactSet then calculated the non-GAAP number, which excluded the tax effects and other special items, and came up with a number of $101.8 billion. Comparing these numbers with the year-earlier period, the Dow posted a decline of 46% on a GAAP basis. It was down 3.3% on a GAAP basis excluding the tax changes and was up 10.5% on a non-GAAP basis excluding tax and other special items.
Revenue rule change Tax was not the only change in this crop of earnings. Jan. 1 was the deadline for most public companies to implement new revenue-recognition rules, and investors got the first look at how companies will be implementing the standards that were approved in 2014, after almost 15 years of work by regulators and companies.
Read: A revenue rule change is coming, and every company will be affected
About 70 companies mentioned the new revenue-recognition standard, ASC 606, when discussing 2018 guidance, according to Audit Analytics. In this sample, 20 companies quantified the impact of the new rules on revenue guidance, and 10 companies quantified an effect on their expected 2018 EPS.
Companies were more likely to quantify the impact if the impact was negative, according to Audit Analytics. 3-D Systems Corp. DDD, +0.92% , for example, announced on Feb. 28 that it would delay filing its annual report for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2017, because it realized it needed additional time to complete its review.
See: With deferred liabilities, Verizon will get earnings benefit from tax bill
Some big companies finished the job early. Microsoft Corp. MSFT, +0.11% adopted the new standards last August, using the full retrospective method, which requires the company to revise and re-audit the numbers for two prior years in order to provide comparable information for investors going forward. Despite having a material impact on the company’s prior-year balance sheets — the change added $6.6 billion and $5.2 billion in 2016 and 2017 to assets and liabilities — the market seemed indifferent to the news.
See now: Uber set on net revenue, but experts say gross would better inform investors
Ford Motor Co. F, -0.52% finished a year in advance, in January 2017, and said in its filings its $530 million positive impact was related to how it accounts for revenue from leased vehicles, although that amount was not material to its results.
Another early adopter, Google parent Alphabet Inc. GOOGL, +1.01% , has already received comment letters from the SEC, asking about the decisions it made when addressing the accounting and disclosure changes and calculating the impact. Those inquiries are closed, for now, with no additional changes required.
Don’t miss: Alphabet vs. the SEC: Google fights YouTube revenue disclosure
Tesla Inc. TSLA, -1.10% reported a $520 million pretax impact from the new revenue standard in its annual report and said the new rules would allow it to post revenue from leased cars much faster.
Read: New accounting rules trim Tesla deficit and promise faster future revenues
But General Motors Co. GM, +0.76% reported a $1 billion negative impact to its equity account from the new accounting standard, saying that certain transactions with daily rental-car companies would qualify for accelerated sales recognition instead of being spread out over time and that it would be required going forward to recognize the cost of sales incentives much sooner.
General Electric Co. GE, -0.17% reported that its adoption of required new revenue-recognition accounting standards would result in a noncash charge to its Jan. 1, 2016, retained earnings balance of approximately $4.2 billion. The announcement that it would “restate” 2016 and 2017 earnings per share to reflect the change , lowering them by about 13 cents and 16 cents, caused widespread confusion and sent the shares tumbling, despite the fact that, like Microsoft, the choice of the full retrospective adoption method is intended to provide more disclosure and more transparency into the impact of the change.
Read now: GE shares zigzag on confusion about impact of new accounting rules
Apple, on the other hand, will be one of the last companies to reflect the impact of the new rules because of its Sept. 30 fiscal-year end. At the end of its first quarter, on Dec 30, the company said in its SEC filing that it would adopt the new revenue standards in the first quarter of 2019, after pushing back from an early adoption in the first quarter of its 2018 fiscal year, and will use the full retrospective method.
Apple said the new standards are not expected to have a material impact on the amount and timing of revenue recognized by the company.
Behind the noise, a strong quarter So after all the extra disclosures, how did companies perform?
The quarter was actually a strong one, with S&P 500 companies reporting the fastest pace of earnings-per-share growth in over seven years, and that’s been followed by an unusually upbeat analyst assessment of the current quarter.
With 99% of the S&P 500 companies having reported results through Thursday morning, aggregate EPS has run up 14.87% from a year ago, the biggest increase since the 17.65% rise for the third quarter of 2011, according to an analysis of FactSet data. All 11 S&P sectors witnessed growth, led by a doubling in EPS for the energy sector and a 44% jump for the materials sector. The worst performer was the real-estate sector, but even that had growth of 4.9%.
On the revenue side, an aggregate rise of 8.30% was the strongest rate of growth since the fourth quarter of 2011, when revenue grew 8.83%. All 11 sectors enjoyed year-over-year increases, led by the energy sector, which saw revenue rise 20.88%, followed by materials, which enjoyed 20.22% revenue growth.
And there is no sign that the earnings-growth momentum is set to slow down. During the first two months of the current quarter, the aggregate bottom-up first-quarter EPS estimate of analysts for the S&P 500 has increased by 5.7% to $36.32 a share, according to FactSet. That’s an about-face from what is typical, as over the past 10 years (40 quarters) the bottom-up EPS estimate has declined by an average of 4% during the first two months of a quarter.
Market strategists point to this strong growth, and the upbeat outlook for the current quarter, as reason to believe the recent volatility in the stock market is just a hiccup in a continuing uptrend.
While concerns over rising interest rates and inflation and worries about a potential trade war sent “shivers” down the stock market’s spine, Liz Ann Sonders, chief investment strategist at Charles Schwab, said in a recent note to clients that the “strong earnings picture” should help underpin the market.
And William Lynch, Hinsdale Associates’ director of investments, said that what investors seem to have forgotten as they obsessed over Federal Reserve monetary policy is “the strength of the fourth-quarter earnings season.”
But a correlation analysis of FactSet data suggest a tempering of such confidence. The correlation coefficient between year-over-year S&P 500 quarterly EPS growth for the past 10 years and the quarterly gain in the S&P 500 index the following quarter was just 0.04, where a 0.00 reading would mean there was no relationship.
That may be why despite the strong fourth-quarter earnings performance and the optimistic outlook for the current quarter, the S&P 500 index SPX, +0.15% has gained just 1.6% so far this year, which puts it on track for the weakest quarterly performance since the index rose just 0.8% during the first quarter of 2016.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, +0.04% has gained 0.5% year to date through midday Thursday, which puts it on track for the worst quarterly performance since the Dow declined 7.6% during the third quarter of 2015.
